edges.description: Neuronal expression of the mutant protein is lethal, supporting its cell-level toxicity.
edges.limitations: An invertebrate overexpression model scored by lethality; it does not reproduce the progressive cerebral/cerebellar neurodegeneration or the regression phenotype. With the pan-neuronal c155-GAL4 driver, wild-type UBTF1 was not lethal (only E210K was); wild-type UBTF1 overexpression was toxic only with the eye driver (Eye3.5-GAL4), causing a small-eye phenotype and semi-lethality, so overexpression toxicity is not E210K-specific in every tissue.

edges.description: Germline Ubtf haploinsufficiency does not reproduce the progressive neurodegeneration of the human syndrome.
edges.limitations: Models Ubtf loss of function rather than the human gain-of-function E210K allele, and produces only modest motor/behavioral signs without overt neurodegeneration.

edges.description: Recapitulates the impaired cooperative UBTF1-SL1 recruitment and altered rDNA transcription attributed to the variant.
edges.limitations: Cell-level readouts from cultured MEFs; the mice do show age-progressive behavioral abnormalities, but the readouts curated here do not capture the cerebral/cerebellar neuroregression of the human disease. Crucially, this is a homozygous (UbtfE210K/E210K) model, so it does not test the heterozygous, single-allele de novo gain-of-function hypothesis on which the human disease rests, and the loss-of-function contribution it points to is in apparent tension with the gain-of-function data from patient fibroblasts.

nodes.description: Homozygous UbtfE210K/E210K mice are viable but develop behavioral abnormalities that worsen with increasing postnatal age (the detailed organismal phenotype is reported elsewhere). The molecular readouts curated here come from cultured UbtfE210K/E210K mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), which show enhanced UBTF1 splice variant and more active rDNA copies but reduced rDNA transcription and reduced SL1 promoter recruitment, interpreted as a loss-of-function contribution partly compensated by enhanced rDNA activation. This informs the molecular mechanism at the preinitiation-complex node.

Heterozygous Ubtf loss-of-function mice show only mild motor and behavioral abnormalities and increased DNA damage in MEFs, but not the severe human neurodegeneration. Because the human variant acts by gain of function, this haploinsufficiency model addresses a different mechanism.
